Written before AD 70, Hebrews says the old covenant is growing old and is ready to vanish away.
ouranos / ge
heaven / earth

Together the two words can mean the created world. In prophetic speech they can also stand for a covenant order, as when Moses calls heaven and earth to witness (Deuteronomy 32:1). This reading links them to the Temple's holy rooms.

Most readers, including many partial preterists, take this as the physical universe, which will end or be renewed at the final judgment. Jesus is contrasting His lasting word with even the most lasting creation.

Matthew 5:18 says not one stroke of the law passes until heaven and earth pass. Hebrews says the old covenant was about to vanish. These fit together if 'heaven and earth' means the covenant world that ended in AD 70.
But of that day and hour knoweth no man

Jesus has just given the generation; now He says the exact day and hour are not known. In this reading, these do not conflict. The disciples knew the event would come in their lifetime, but not the day. So they had to stay ready at all times, prepared to leave for the mountains when they saw the signs.
The precise timing of the siege and fall, which came within the generation but at a moment no one could name in advance.
After the resurrection Jesus again told the disciples that times and seasons were in the Father's authority.
The Jerusalem believers left in time, which shows readiness without a fixed date.
Many readers see verse 36 as a turn to a different, still-future 'day': the final return of Christ, which has no signs. Others think the whole discourse is about one event.
'That day' points back to the events just described. Knowing the generation but not the day was exactly the disciples' situation.
As in the days of Noah
as the days of Noe were

Jesus compares His coming to the flood. In Noah's day God waited while the ark was built, but the people did not repent, and judgment came on that generation. In this reading, God gave Jerusalem about forty years after the cross to hear the gospel. When most leaders refused, judgment came on that generation too, just as it came on Noah's.
The judgment of AD 70, which this reading identifies with the Parousia, after about forty years of gospel preaching in Judea.
Peter says God waited patiently in Noah's day while the ark was built, and only eight people were saved.
God set a limit of one hundred and twenty years before the flood.
parousia
coming, presence, arrival
The word was used for the visit of a king or official to a city. It appears in Matthew only in this chapter (24:3, 27, 37, 39). This reading takes it as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem.
Futurist readers see the days of Noah as a picture of the world just before Christ's bodily return, with people living normally and unprepared.
Noah's flood was a judgment on one generation. Jesus applies it to 'this generation', so the comparison fits the end of Jerusalem's age.
Eating, drinking, marrying
eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage

Life went on as normal before the flood. In this reading, life in Jerusalem also went on as normal after the cross. The priests kept offering daily sacrifices, as if the final sacrifice had not been made. Hebrews says the old system was a copy and a shadow. Daily routine hid the danger, and few saw that the old covenant age was ending.
Temple worship continued until the daily sacrifice stopped during the siege in summer AD 70, shortly before the Temple burned.
Josephus records that the daily sacrifice failed on the seventeenth of Tammuz (July AD 70) for lack of men to offer it.
The way into the holy place was not yet open while the first tabernacle was still standing.
Futurist readers apply this to the general spirit of the world before Christ returns: carelessness rather than open wickedness.
Jesus was speaking about His hearers' own world. In Jerusalem the normal routine included Temple sacrifices that continued until the siege.
The flood took them all away
the flood came, and took them all away

This is a key point in the fulfilled reading. In the flood, the people who were 'taken away' were the wicked, swept away in judgment. Noah and his family were the ones left. So in this picture, being taken is not a rescue. It means being removed in judgment, just as Jerusalem's rebels were removed in AD 70.
The killing and capture of Jerusalem's population in AD 70.
Josephus counts 97,000 people taken captive during the whole war and gives a very large number of dead.
Every living thing was wiped out; only Noah and those with him in the ark were left.
Many futurist readers agree that the flood 'took away' the wicked, but see this as the world's judgment at Christ's return.
In the flood the wicked were removed and the righteous remained. That pattern happened to Jerusalem within the generation.
Two in the field
the one shall be taken, and the other left

Following verse 39, this reading takes 'taken' as taken in judgment, like the flood. Farm workers out in the open fields were exposed when the Roman army arrived. Some were seized as captives, and others escaped. Jesus warns that people side by side could meet very different ends. Rome often took captives as slaves.
The Roman army swept through Judea from AD 67 to 70, killing and capturing people across the countryside.
After the fall, captives over seventeen were sent in chains to work in Egypt, and many were sent to the provinces to die in arenas.
Josephus counts 97,000 captives in the war.
paralambano
to take along, to take with oneself

Verse 39 uses a different verb for the flood 'taking away' (airo). Futurist readers note that paralambano is used in John 14:3 for Christ 'receiving' His people. Preterists answer that context, the flood parallel, decides the meaning.
Pre-tribulation readers often see the rapture here: believers taken to Christ, unbelievers left. Others take it as the separation at Christ's return.
Jesus has just said the flood 'took them all away'. In that picture the ones taken are the ones judged. Luke 17:37 adds that the taken go where the vultures gather.
Two women at the mill
Two women shall be grinding at the mill

Grinding grain for bread was daily work for women in every home. In this reading, Jesus warns that ordinary work would not protect anyone when the army came. Women, like men, could be taken as captives. The disciples were to make sure their families stayed alert and ready to flee.
The capture and sale of women and children when Jerusalem and the towns of Judea fell (AD 67-70).
Josephus says the Romans sold the people, with their wives and children, at a very low price because there were so many.
After Jerusalem's first fall, young men were forced to grind at the mill.
Futurist readers see the sudden separation of believers and unbelievers at Christ's coming, in the middle of ordinary life.
The setting is a village of first-century Judea, and the warning is to flee in time. The judgment that came was the Roman war.
Watch
ye know not what hour your Lord doth come

Because the hour was not known, the disciples had to keep watch. In this reading, this is practical advice about real danger. About forty years would pass, and by then the disciples would have families and churches to protect. Watching meant staying faithful in the mission while being ready to act on Jesus' warning.
The Jerusalem church's flight before the war, which this reading sees as obedience to the call to watch.
The believers in Jerusalem left the city before the war and went to Pella in Perea.
Jesus told them to watch and pray, so that they could escape what was about to happen.
Most Christians apply this to every generation, which should live ready for Christ's return at any time.
The command was first for the disciples facing a real war. Its lesson of faithful readiness still applies to all believers.
The thief in the night
if the goodman of the house had known

A thief does not announce when he will come. In this reading, the coming judgment would break in like a thief, and the Roman army would arrive on the city suddenly. The owner who watches is not caught. The disciples were to live normally but keep watch.
Titus arrived just before Passover in AD 70, and the pilgrims who had come for the feast were trapped inside the walls.
Josephus explains that the crowds had come from the whole country for the feast and were suddenly shut in by the war.
Jesus warns a first-century church that He will come like a thief if they do not watch.
Futurist readers see Christ's return coming suddenly on an unready world. Paul's 'thief' language is often read the same way.
Paul told the Thessalonians that the day would not surprise them, because they were children of light. The warning was for people who could live to see it.
Be ready
Therefore be ye also ready

This reading asks who is speaking and to whom. Jesus speaks to Peter, James, John and Andrew. 'You also be ready' was a call to them. They did not know the hour, but they knew it would come within their lifetime. The Son of Man would come when they did not expect, so readiness had to be constant.
The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, within the lifetime of the disciples who heard the warning.
Mark names the four listeners: Peter, James, John and Andrew.
When they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies, they would know its desolation was near.
Futurist readers see a timeless call for all believers to be ready for Christ's bodily return, whenever it may come.
The call was first a life-saving warning for the disciples' own generation. Readiness and faithfulness remain the lesson for us.
Who then is a faithful and wise servant

Jesus now turns from warning to stewardship. The servant set over the household gives food at the right time. In this reading, the servants are the apostles and leaders of the first church, who had to feed God's people through about forty hard years before the end came. Jesus later called them friends, not only servants.
The apostolic ministry from Pentecost (about AD 30-33) to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
Jesus tells Peter to feed His sheep.
Paul says stewards must be found faithful.
Futurist and most other readers apply the servant to all church leaders and believers in every age until Christ returns.
The parable first addressed the apostles, who were left in charge until the Master came within their generation. Every steward can still learn from it.
Blessed when the master comes
Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh

The servant who is found faithful at the master's coming is blessed. In this reading, Jesus encourages His disciples, as a group and one by one, to keep going until His coming. The blessing goes to the one who keeps on working, not to the one who guesses the date. This leads into the parables of Matthew 25.
The faithful believers who kept serving through the persecutions and wars of AD 30-70.
Jesus tells a first-century church to be faithful until death and promises the crown of life.
Paul, near the end of his life, says he has finished the race and kept the faith.
Most readers see a blessing for every faithful believer when Christ returns at the end of history.
The promise was to people who would see the coming in their lifetime. The principle of faithful service is the same today.
Ruler over all his goods
he shall make him ruler over all his goods

The reward for faithful service is greater responsibility. In this reading, the faithful servants share in Christ's rule. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones in the 'regeneration'. Some interpreters link this to the original call to have dominion in Genesis 1:28, now given to the church.
The church's place in Christ's kingdom after the old covenant order passed away in AD 70.
Jesus gives His disciples a kingdom, as the Father gave one to Him.
The one who overcomes will sit with Christ on His throne.
Futurist readers place the reward in the future, for example ruling with Christ in a millennial kingdom after His return.
Jesus said the Twelve would judge Israel 'in the regeneration'. This reading sees that new order as beginning when the old covenant age ended.
My lord delays his coming
My lord delayeth his coming

Jesus calls the servant who says 'my master is delaying' evil. In this reading, the fault is to treat the coming as far off and so to live carelessly. Some preterists also see a warning against speaking as if Christ's promise to come within that generation had failed.
Scoffers in the decades before AD 70 who asked, 'Where is the promise of His coming?'
Peter warns of scoffers who ask where the promise of His coming is.
Hebrews says that in a very little while the coming one will come and will not delay.
Many readers note that the parable itself assumes some delay (compare Matthew 25:5, 19). The evil servant's sin is misusing the delay, not expecting one.
Hebrews promised that He would not delay. In this reading the delay was short, within a generation, and the servant's mistake was to think it long.
Beating fellow servants
shall begin to smite his fellowservants

The evil servant turns on his fellow servants and joins the drunkards. In this reading, the picture fits the years before AD 70. Jerusalem's leaders persecuted the church. Later the city's own factions fought and killed one another. Instead of feeding the household, its leaders wounded it.
Persecution of Jerusalem's believers (AD 30-62) and the civil war between the factions inside the city (AD 67-70).
The high priest Ananus had James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in AD 62.
The rival leaders John and Simon fought each other and burned the city's grain stores, which led to famine.
Most readers see a picture of any unfaithful leader in the church who abuses others and lives for pleasure while waiting for Christ.
Matthew 23:34 has just said that Jerusalem's leaders would beat and kill Jesus' messengers. This verse fits that warning.
An hour he is not aware of
shall come in a day when he looketh not

The careless servant is caught by surprise. In this reading, the master's coming matched the Roman army's arrival, which came on people who were still sure of rescue. Many expected God to deliver the city even as it burned, and they had no way out.
The fall of the Temple and city in AD 70, when many still expected rescue until the end.
A false prophet told the people to go up to the Temple to receive signs of deliverance; about 6,000 died when the portico burned.
Tacitus says many Jews believed ancient writings foretold that men from Judea would rule the world at that very time.
Futurist readers see the sudden return of Christ catching unfaithful professing believers unprepared.
The people of Jerusalem looked for rescue, not judgment. Jesus warned that the master's coming would surprise those who were not watching.
Cut asunder, with the hypocrites
shall cut him asunder, and appoint him his portion

The punishment is severe: the servant is 'cut in two' and given a place with the hypocrites. In Matthew 23 Jesus called the scribes and Pharisees 'hypocrites' seven times. So in this reading, the evil servant shares the fate of Jerusalem's leaders. Weeping and gnashing of teeth is what Jesus had said would happen to 'the sons of the kingdom' who were cast out.
The destruction of Jerusalem's leadership in AD 70.
Jesus begins a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees, calling them hypocrites.
The sons of the kingdom will be thrown out, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.
dichotomeo
to cut in two

The word is used in the Greek Old Testament for cutting up a sacrifice (Exodus 29:17). Some take it literally as a cruel death; others take it as being cut off, severely punished. Hypokrites first meant a stage actor, someone playing a part.
Most readers see final judgment on false or unfaithful believers when Christ returns.
Jesus links the evil servant to the 'hypocrites' He had just judged in Matthew 23, and that judgment was to fall on 'this generation'.
The ten virgins
Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him

There were no chapter breaks in Matthew, so this parable continues the same talk to the same disciples. The bridegroom is Jesus. Some interpreters take the lamp as God's word and the oil as the Holy Spirit. The point is readiness: wise people prepare for a delay, but foolish people do not. In this reading, the wedding is the union of Christ and His church, completed when the old covenant age ended.
The coming of the Bridegroom, which this reading places at AD 70, after a 'delay' of about forty years.
The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.
Jesus had just told a parable of a king's wedding feast, ending with the city of the murderers burned.
Futurist readers see believers or Israel needing readiness for Christ's return. Many apply the 'shut door' to the final judgment.
The parable ends with the same call as Matthew 24:42, 'Watch', and so it shares that chapter's timeframe.
After a long time the lord of those servants cometh

A master entrusts money to his servants and returns 'after a long time' to settle accounts. Two servants trade and double what they were given. The third hides his talent out of fear. In this reading, the long time is the forty years before AD 70. The servants who received the kingdom had to make it bear fruit, while the old order lost what it had.
The accounting at AD 70, when the kingdom was taken from the unfruitful and given to a fruitful people (Matthew 21:43).
Jesus told the leaders that the kingdom would be taken from them and given to a people who bear its fruit.
Luke's similar parable was told because the people thought the kingdom would appear at once.
Most readers apply the parable to all believers, who will give account at Christ's return for how they used His gifts.
The 'long time' is long for a lifetime, not for twenty centuries. The parable follows the same 'watch' teaching aimed at the disciples' generation.
When the Son of man shall come in his glory

The Son of Man comes in glory with His angels and sits on His throne. He gathers the nations and separates them. Jesus had already said He would come in glory and reward each person while some of His hearers still lived (Matthew 16:27-28). In this reading, the scene shows Christ's reign over all nations beginning with the judgment on Jerusalem. The 'least of these' are His messengers (Matthew 10:42).
The judgment of AD 70 and the kingdom opened to all nations. Full preterists place the whole scene there; partial preterists place it at a final judgment.
The Son of Man will come in His Father's glory with His angels and reward each person by what they have done.
Some standing there would not taste death before they saw the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.
Most Christians, including partial preterists, see the final judgment of all people at the end of history, since verse 46 speaks of eternal life and eternal punishment.
The same 'coming in glory with angels' was promised within His hearers' lifetime. In this reading the judgment that began then has eternal results.
The sun darkened, the moon without light, the stars falling

The prophets used this picture when a ruling power fell. Isaiah used it for the fall of Babylon, and Ezekiel used it for the fall of Egypt. In Joseph's dream the sun, moon and stars stood for his family, so they can stand for rulers. The fulfilled reading takes the verse as the collapse of Jerusalem's ruling order in AD 70, not as a failure of the physical sky.
The Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven

In the Old Testament God "rides on a cloud" when He comes to judge a nation, as He did against Egypt. No one saw God's body in those events. They saw His judgment in history. The fulfilled reading holds that Jesus claimed this divine role before the high priest, and that His generation saw it when Rome destroyed the city and temple.
Heaven and earth passing away

This reading takes "heaven and earth" as covenant and temple language, not the physical universe. Josephus says the tabernacle was laid out as a picture of the world: the parts open to the priests stood for land and sea, and the inner room stood for heaven (Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7). Some interpreters therefore map the Holy of Holies to heaven, the Holy Place to earth and the outer court to sea, and they hold that this "world" passed away when the temple fell. Jesus' words, by contrast, would remain.
The abomination of desolation standing in the holy place

Daniel speaks of a defiling thing that stops the sacrifices and leaves the sanctuary desolate. Luke's parallel explains it plainly: Jerusalem surrounded by armies. The fulfilled reading sees the Roman armies, with their idol-like standards, as the defiling power. Some also include the Zealots, who turned the temple into a fortress and shed blood in its courts (Josephus, Jewish War 4.3.7-10).
Where the carcass is, there the eagles gather

The Greek word can mean eagle or vulture. Literally, the dead of the siege lay unburied for the birds. Symbolically, the eagle was the emblem on the Roman legions' standards, and Moses had warned of a nation "like an eagle" coming against a disobedient Israel. Josephus records that the soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them while the temple burned (Josephus, Jewish War 6.6.1).
Lightning flashing from east to west

The point of the picture is that His coming would be public and impossible to miss. It would not be hidden in the desert or in secret rooms, where false messiahs gathered followers. In the Psalms lightning goes with God's coming in judgment. Some fulfilled-reading writers add a geographical link to the Roman advance, but that detail is debated; the main point is visibility and speed.
The fig tree putting out leaves

Leaves on a fig tree show that summer is near. In the same way, the signs Jesus listed would show the disciples that the city's fall was near, so they could leave in time. Luke says "the fig tree and all the trees", so this reading takes it as an ordinary seasonal lesson, not a code for a modern nation. Some also recall the barren fig tree Jesus cursed in Matthew 21 as a picture of a fruitless temple system.
A great trumpet and the gathering of the elect from the four winds

In Israel trumpets called the people to gather, and Isaiah speaks of a great trumpet that brings the scattered home to worship. The Greek word for angels also means messengers. The fulfilled reading takes the verse as the gospel call going out through God's messengers, gathering His people from every nation into the new covenant community once the old order fell.

Noah's neighbours went on eating, drinking and marrying, and ignored the warning until the flood came. God had waited patiently before the flood. This reading sees a parallel in the roughly forty years between Jesus' warning and AD 70. In the flood it was the wicked who were "taken away", so this reading takes "one taken" as taken in judgment, such as captured by Rome, not rescued.
The thief who comes at an unknown hour

A thief does not announce the hour he will come, so the owner must stay awake. The picture stresses that the exact time was unknown, even though the generation was known. The fulfilled reading applies it to the believers of that generation, who had to stay ready to flee at short notice. Paul and Revelation use the same picture for a coming their first readers had to watch for.
The bridegroom arriving at midnight

In Jewish custom a betrothal came first, and then, after a waiting time, the groom came to take his bride home. Jesus called Himself the bridegroom. Some fulfilled-reading writers see the years between the cross and AD 70 as that waiting time, ending when Christ came for His bride, the church, as the old covenant passed. The lamps and oil call for faithful readiness through a dark and long night.
The shepherd separating the sheep from the goats

Ezekiel pictures God as a shepherd who judges between sheep and goats among His own flock. The King gathers "all the nations", which shows that the kingdom is no longer limited to Israel. Here fulfilled readers differ. Full preterists place this judgment at the coming in AD 70, while partial preterists, with most churches, read it as the final judgment still to come.
The end of the age

The Greek word aion means an age or era, not the physical world. The fulfilled reading takes the disciples' question as asking about the end of the Mosaic covenant age, which they linked with the temple's fall. New Testament writers spoke of their own time as the end of the ages, and Hebrews describes the old covenant as about to vanish.

The word for sorrows means labour pains. Pain in labour grows stronger, but it leads to new life. This reading sees the wars, famines and earthquakes before AD 70 as the pains that came before the new covenant age was fully born. Paul and the prophets use the same picture for the birth of a new people.
till the Son of man be come
Jesus told the Twelve they would not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man came. The fulfilled reading takes this as a coming within their working lives.
some standing here, which shall not taste of death
The coming with angels to repay each person is tied to the lifetime of some who heard Him. Others read verse 28 as the Transfiguration, the resurrection or Pentecost.
All these things shall come upon this generation
Spoken to the leaders in the temple, just before the discourse. It sets the time frame that Matthew 24:34 repeats.
This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled
The central time text of the discourse. The fulfilled reading takes 'this generation' as Jesus' own contemporaries.
Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man
Jesus told the high priest and the council that they themselves would see Him seated at God's right hand and coming on the clouds.
The night is far spent, the day is at hand
Paul tells the Roman church that their salvation is nearer than when they first believed.
shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly
A promise of victory to the believers in Rome, described as coming soon.
the time is short
Paul advises the Corinthians in light of the shortened time and says the present form of this world is passing away.
upon whom the ends of the world are come
The Greek speaks of the ends of the ages. Paul places his own generation at the close of the ages.
The Lord is at hand.
Some read this as nearness in time, others as nearness in presence. The fulfilled reading takes it as time.
he that shall come will come, and will not tarry
Drawing on Habakkuk 2:3, the writer tells suffering believers that the coming One will arrive in a very little while.
the coming of the Lord draweth nigh
James adds that the Judge is standing at the door. The fulfilled reading links this to the judgment on Jerusalem.
the end of all things is at hand
Peter urges sober prayer because the end is near. The fulfilled reading takes 'all things' as the old covenant order.
Little children, it is the last time
John says that many antichrists have already appeared, and that this shows it is the last hour.
things which must shortly come to pass
The book opens by saying its events must happen soon. The fulfilled reading stresses that this covers all of them, not only some.
for the time is at hand
A blessing on those who read and keep the prophecy, because the time is near.
Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book
John must not seal his book because the time is near. Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4).
Surely I come quickly.
The last promise in the Bible. Futurist readers take 'quickly' as sudden or certain; the fulfilled reading takes it as soon.
Jesus foretells the temple's fall

On the Mount of Olives, in the last week before the cross (about AD 30, or AD 33 on another dating), Jesus tells four disciples that not one stone of the temple will be left on another. He adds that this generation will not pass away before it happens.

Fifty days after the resurrection the Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem. Jews "from every nation under heaven" hear the gospel, and the message begins to spread across the Roman world (Acts 2).
Stephen is stoned
Stephen is put to death in Jerusalem (Acts 7), probably in the early or middle 30s. A wide persecution follows, and believers scatter through Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1).
James son of Zebedee is killed
King Herod Agrippa I has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword and arrests Peter (Acts 12:1-3). Agrippa dies the same year.
Theudas leads people to the Jordan
Under the governor Fadus (AD 44-46), Theudas claims to be a prophet and promises to part the Jordan. Roman cavalry kill many of his followers (Josephus, Antiquities 20.5.1; compare Acts 5:36).

Agabus had foretold a great famine over "all the world", and it came in the days of Claudius (Acts 11:28). Judea suffered badly around AD 46-48 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.2.5 and 20.5.2). The church in Antioch sent relief to Judea (Acts 11:29-30).
Paul before Gallio at Corinth

On his mission across the Roman world, Paul is brought before Gallio, governor of Achaia (Acts 18:12-17). An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term to about AD 51-52, which helps fix the timeline of Paul's travels.
The Egyptian false prophet

Under the governor Felix, a man called "the Egyptian" gathers followers on the Mount of Olives and promises that the walls of Jerusalem will fall. Felix scatters them (Josephus, Jewish War 2.13.5; compare Acts 21:38).
The gospel heard "in all the world"

Writing to Rome around AD 57, Paul says the Romans' faith is reported in all the world (Romans 1:8). A few years later he says the gospel has been preached to every creature under heaven (Colossians 1:23).
Earthquakes in Asia and Italy

Laodicea is ruined by an earthquake and rebuilds without Roman help (Tacitus, Annals 14.27, AD 60). In AD 62 an earthquake strikes Pompeii in Campania (Tacitus, Annals 15.22; Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Seneca was Gallio's brother.
James the Just is killed
Between two Roman governors, the high priest Ananus has James, the brother of Jesus, and others stoned in Jerusalem (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1).
